name: Ben Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your firm. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the moulds the concrete gets poured into. Right now we're on a fourteen-storey block of flats by the river for Castell Concrete, and my gang does a floor every eight or nine days. I'm on site at half six, we strip yesterday's panels, fix new ones, and by afternoon the steel fixers are waiting on us. I like it when a pour goes off clean and you see a whole floor that wasn't there last week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you in it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cold wears me out, and the wind up on the deck in January is no joke. What keeps me in it is the gang and the money: with union rates and overtime I'm on more than most lads my age, and Sana (my partner) and I have nearly ten months saved plus a deposit for a flat. I'm a union member and I go to branch meetings, because I've seen what non-union sites pay. I don't use any of the AI stuff, I've still got a phone with a cracked screen and that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Every year some bloke in a suit says the site's going to be run by computers, and every year I'm still fixing ply by hand. I'd probably post a photo of the deck with a joke about where the robot is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the job stays mine. The thing that actually worries me is the developers, not computers. If the housing market dips, Castell lays off the newest gangs first, and AI won't change that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, keep the overtime and keep putting money aside for the flat. I'd keep going to the branch meetings, because pay rises come from the union, not from technology. Maybe Sana and I would finally put an offer in on a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like a storm that never turned up. It'd feel normal, and normal is pretty good for me right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the housing market. How much does that worry you, separate from any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Two winters ago half the cranes on the river went quiet for three months and I did patch work on a car park to get by. With our savings we'd be fine, but I don't like dipping into the flat money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the office side of Castell change at all, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the people doing rotas and orders would use it for emails. That's not me. My gang leader Marco still writes the cut list on a bit of ply, and that's how I like it.

say: I'd tell everyone **told you so**, because the site still runs on hands.
I'd post a **joke photo** of the deck asking where the robot went.
think: My **job stays mine** in this picture, with no real change.
The real risk is a **housing slump**, when Castell lays off newer gangs first.
do: **Keep the overtime** at Castell and carry on on the river block.
Put an **offer on a flat** with Sana using the deposit they've saved.
Keep going to **branch meetings** to push for the next pay rise.
feel: **Relieved**, like a storm that never turned up.
S0.quote: My gang leader Marco still writes the cut list on a bit of ply, and that's how I like it.
fieldNote: Ben trusts the **union** far more than any technology to protect his pay.
His real worry is the **building cycle**, not AI; he remembers a quiet winter.
Strong savings make him **secure**, and he says so plainly.

steps.text: Keep working overtime on the Castell river block
Keep going to monthly union branch meetings
Put an offer on a flat with Sana this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to worry, not us. At the branch I'd push for the union to get ahead of it, so if they bring in any robot kit it comes with rules. Online I'd say the same: keep it off our backs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'll get to us slower but it'll get to us. If the planners and buyers get cut, the site managers will start using apps to time us, and that's what gets under my skin. My hands are fine for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still keep going, but I'd put more aside, maybe an extra two hundred a month. I'd want the branch to write AI and robot rules into the next site agreement. I'm not going on a course to learn AI, that's not happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit edgy. I'm not scared for this year, but I'd feel the ground starting to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the site would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsty in the site office does all the orders and the deliveries. If software books the concrete and the steel, Kirsty in the site office is gone, and she's got two kids. That's what makes me angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn AI. If the firm handed you a tablet with a new app, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, grudgingly, like the sign-in app we already have. But I'd want the union to have checked it isn't just there to clock how many minutes I spend on a cup of tea.

say: I'd say **office jobs** feel this first, not the people on the deck.
I'd push the **branch** to set rules before any robot kit arrives on site.
think: My hands-on work is **safe for years**, but tracking apps could follow.
Office staff like **Kirsty** who books deliveries would lose out first.
do: Put an **extra £200 a month** into savings on top of the flat deposit.
Ask the branch to write **AI rules** into the next site agreement.
Refuse any **AI course**, and use new apps only when forced.
feel: **Edgy**, sensing the ground start to move under the site.
S1.quote: If software books the concrete and the steel, Kirsty in the site office is gone, and she's got two kids.
fieldNote: His anger is about **colleagues**, not himself, which fits his union outlook.
He fears **monitoring apps** more than robots in this picture.
He flatly rejects learning AI, a **resistant** streak even when pushed.

steps.text: Add £200 a month to savings on top of the deposit
Ask the branch to put AI rules in the site agreement
Carry on formwork at Castell without any AI course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates tech companies. I'd be at every branch meeting and I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd tell people we need the government to step in now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I've got until about 2031, because the robots come later than the thinking stuff. That's me at thirty-two. Castell's planners and quantity surveyors would go in 2028, and then they'd be pricing jobs around the day robots can do formwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car and no holiday, and hold off on the flat until we know what's what. I'd be pushing the union hard for a deal on retraining money and redundancy terms. Sana's a nurse, so I'd lean on her steadier job for a bit if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach, to be honest. Three years sounds like a lot until you count it in winters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sana the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying the flat yet, and I'd hate saying it. We've been saving for five years. I'd say we've got the money, we just shouldn't lock it into a mortgage until we know if I've got work in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't want to learn AI. Is there anything you would retrain for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, maybe I'd go for a crane ticket or something still hands-on. But by the time I'd finished it the robots are only a couple of years off, so I don't know. I'd rather fight for my job than chase a new one.

say: I'd say this is what you get when **nobody regulates** the tech companies.
I'd go to **every branch meeting** and join any march going.
think: I've got until about **2031** before robots can do formwork.
Castell would **price future jobs** around the day robots arrive, which scares me.
do: **Freeze big spending**, so no new car and no holiday this year.
Put the **flat purchase on hold** and keep the deposit as cash.
Push the union for **redundancy terms** and retraining money in writing.
feel: **Sick in the stomach**, with three years feeling short counted in winters.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a lot until you count it in winters.
fieldNote: He clearly sees the **3-year gap** between AGI and robots and counts it in winters.
Pausing the flat is his **hardest decision**; five years of saving sit behind it.
He would rather **fight than retrain**, true to his resistant profile.

steps.text: Skip the new car and the summer holiday
Put the flat purchase on hold and keep the deposit
Push the branch for written redundancy and retraining terms
Lean on Sana's nursing pay if site work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse for the government this time. I'd want the union campaigning from day one for rules on robots on site. I'd be saying that online too, which I don't usually bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three for the robots puts me at about thirty-five. That's still young enough to start again, which is what bothers me, because I don't want to start again. But it's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage is something Sana could cover on her own if it came to that. I'd save hard and maybe vote for whoever promises a proper plan for workers. I'd keep fixing formwork as long as there's formwork to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not panicking. It's like seeing a bad forecast for next week instead of tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller flat mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A one-bed instead of the two-bed we wanted, and further out, past the ring road. Sana's not going to love the commute. But I'd sleep better knowing her wage covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you try the AI tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union ran a course and said it'd protect us, maybe. But only if it was the union. I'm not going on some company course where they teach me to train my own replacement.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so the government has no excuse this time.
I'd back the union **campaigning from day one** for rules on site robots.
think: Robots by **2034** puts me at thirty-five, young enough to start over.
I **don't want** to start again, which bothers me more than the timing.
do: Buy a **smaller one-bed** past the ring road that Sana's wage could cover.
Vote for whoever offers a **real plan for workers** at the next election.
Keep fixing formwork and **save hard** while the work is there.
feel: **Worried but steady**, like a bad forecast for next week, not tomorrow.
S3.quote: I'm not going on some company course where they teach me to train my own replacement.
fieldNote: Extra warning time lets him **still buy a flat**, just smaller and safer.
He would only **learn AI** through a union course, never through the firm.
His deepest fear is **starting over**, not being broke.

steps.text: Buy a one-bed past the ring road instead of a two-bed
Vote for the party with a real plan for site workers
Save hard from overtime every month
Keep working formwork at Castell while it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's actually do it properly. Training, rules, a share of the money for the workers. I'd say it in the canteen and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be thirty-nine or forty when the robots come. That's halfway through a working life, and I've got no idea what I'd do. But ten years is a long time, and lots of things I worried about at seventeen never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the two-bed flat we wanted. I'd keep doing formwork and maybe, around year five, look at becoming a site supervisor, since that's still people managing people. I'd stay in the union and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's far enough off that I'd mostly just get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather fight than retrain. Does a decade change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. With ten years I could do it at my own pace, and I wouldn't feel like I was being pushed out. I still wouldn't pick an AI job though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a seventeen-year-old who wants to start formwork today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a seventeen-year-old to do it, but to get a supervisor's ticket by thirty. The trade's good money and good people. Just don't be the last one on the deck when the robots turn up.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough time to do this properly.
I'd push for **training, rules** and a fair share of the money for workers.
think: I'd be about **forty** when robots come, halfway through my working life.
Plenty of my **teenage worries** never happened, so I'd stay level about this one.
do: Buy the **two-bed flat** with Sana as planned.
Look at a **site supervisor ticket** around year five.
Stay in the union and keep **saving steadily** from overtime.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, far enough off to get on with life.
S4.quote: Just don't be the last one on the deck when the robots turn up.
fieldNote: A decade softens his **resistance**; he'd retrain at his own pace.
He picks **site supervision** because it is still people managing people.
The flat goes back to the **original plan**, showing how much timing matters to him.

steps.text: Buy the two-bed flat with Sana as first planned
Take a site supervisor course around year five
Stay an active member of the union branch
Keep saving a set amount from overtime each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It's the only one where I'd tell Sana we can't buy the flat. What would help is the union having a deal ready before it happens: proper redundancy money, paid retraining, and a say over when robots come on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who aren't in a union. I'm lucky, I've got savings and a branch behind me. The lads on agency contracts down the road have no savings and no union, and they'd be first out the gate in every one of these pictures.

headlineQuote: The lads on agency contracts down the road have no savings and no union, and they'd be first out the gate in every one of these pictures.
portrait: Ben is a 27-year-old **formwork carpenter** on a fourteen-storey river block, living with **Sana**, a nurse.
He has strong **savings**, a flat **deposit**, union rates and overtime, and never uses AI.
He trusts the **union** over any technology and blames unregulated tech firms and developers.
His mood tracks the **robot date**: calm with AI Plateau, anxious when robots arrive by 2031 or 2034.
The **flat purchase** is his test: bought, shrunk or paused depending on how much warning there is.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would force him to put the **flat** on hold.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** in advance with redundancy money, **paid retraining** and a say over robots.
